title: A schedule that pays more
prompt: Your employer offers an extra assignment for this year. It would add $2,400 gross pay, but take two evenings most weeks. A family commitment already uses one evening.
context: The extra income is taxable. Time costs continue even when the assignment is inconvenient.

choices.label: Accept the full assignment
choices.text: Earn $2,400 gross this year and give up regular recovery time.
choices.feedback: Income rises at settlement, but your personal schedule becomes much tighter. More money did not create more hours.

choices.label: Negotiate a smaller assignment
choices.text: Earn $900 gross and protect one of the evenings.
choices.feedback: The fictional employer accepts a smaller role. You gain less income while preserving some time.

choices.label: Keep your current workload
choices.text: Decline the extra pay and keep the existing schedule.
choices.feedback: You protect time and give up extra income. Your regular paycheck is unchanged.

title: The training your employer will not cover
prompt: A useful training course costs $1,200. It could strengthen your work, but your employer has no reimbursement budget. The course meets after work for several months.
context: Training does not guarantee a promotion or a raise.

choices.label: Pay for the course
choices.text: Spend $1,200 and commit evenings to learning.
choices.feedback: You gained practice and a credential in the story. The cash and time costs are real within the model; no automatic raise was added.

choices.label: Build a slower learning plan
choices.text: Spend $200 on materials and ask for monthly feedback.
choices.feedback: Your progress is slower and less structured, but your finances take a smaller hit.

choices.label: Wait a year
choices.text: Protect cash and focus on current duties.
choices.feedback: You keep your cash available. This opportunity passes without making you unqualified for your current job.

title: A health problem interrupts work
prompt: You need time away from work. In this fictional job, the available paid leave covers only part of the absence. Medical costs are handled in the normal budget; this decision concerns lost income and recovery.
context: This is a scenario benefit policy, not a claim about all employers in your career.

choices.label: Take the needed recovery time
choices.text: Lose $1,800 of gross pay this year; prioritize recovery.
choices.feedback: Recovery protects your well-being, while lost pay tightens the year’s budget.

choices.label: Arrange temporary shorter days
choices.text: Lose $900 gross and return with a reduced workload.
choices.feedback: The arrangement reduces the pay loss but leaves less room for rest.

choices.label: Use temporary help at home
choices.text: Spend $650 to reduce outside responsibilities; still lose $900 gross.
choices.feedback: Paid help protects recovery time. It cannot replace your missing wages.

title: An error needs to be corrected
prompt: You discover a mistake in work already delivered. It can be fixed, but other people are relying on the current version. Reporting it will be uncomfortable and may delay a deadline.
context: The model rewards taking responsibility, while still recognizing time and reputation costs.

choices.label: Report it and propose a correction
choices.text: Work through the issue with the affected people.
choices.feedback: You make the correction visible. Handling it responsibly still costs time and creates short-term pressure.

choices.label: Ask a colleague to check first
choices.text: Get a second review before contacting everyone.
choices.feedback: A second check clarifies the scope. You must still communicate what needs changing.

choices.label: Quietly replace it without notice
choices.text: Save an awkward conversation, but leave others using the old work.
choices.feedback: Conflicting versions cause more confusion. Avoiding the conversation creates a larger work problem.

title: A job offer across town
prompt: A different employer offers $3,000 more gross pay each year beginning now. The commute would add $160 a month in transport and reduce free time. A move is not required.
context: A higher salary is not the same as a larger spending margin.

choices.label: Take the new offer
choices.text: Add $3,000 gross this year; increase transport by $160/month going forward.
choices.feedback: The commute uses much of the after-withholding raise. Future extra salary is tracked in the follow-up decision.

choices.label: Stay and ask for development opportunities
choices.text: Keep current pay and commute.
choices.feedback: You keep a familiar routine. A development conversation does not guarantee higher pay.

choices.label: Negotiate a one-year trial arrangement
choices.text: Add $1,200 gross this year and $60/month in transport.
choices.feedback: The fictional employer accepts a narrower trial. The smaller pay increase has a smaller commute cost.

title: Your new job is no longer new
prompt: You accepted the across-town role. Its $3,000 gross pay premium continues, and the higher transport cost remains in your budget. You can change the arrangement this year.
context: This follow-up carries forward the consequences of your earlier choice.

choices.label: Keep the role
choices.text: Keep the $3,000 annual premium and the recurring transport cost.
choices.feedback: The premium continues for this year, alongside the recurring commute cost.

choices.label: Return to a nearby role
choices.text: Give up the premium and remove the added $160 monthly commute cost.
choices.feedback: You end the arrangement. Returning to nearby work lowers costs but does not keep the premium.

choices.label: Negotiate some travel support
choices.text: Keep the premium; cut the added commute spending by $60/month and end the trial.
choices.feedback: The fictional employer supports some travel. The remaining commute cost stays; the special premium is not assumed beyond this trial year.

title: Your team is short staffed
prompt: Two positions are temporarily unfilled. You are asked to cover more tasks without an immediate raise. Your usual responsibilities have not disappeared.
context: Good planning can help, but cannot make an unlimited workload sustainable.

choices.label: Agree on priorities with your supervisor
choices.text: Ask which tasks can wait and document the plan.
choices.feedback: Some tasks are delayed deliberately. Clear priorities reduce confusion, but the staffing problem remains.

choices.label: Try to cover everything
choices.text: Work extra unpaid hours to keep every deadline.
choices.feedback: You keep work moving for now at a substantial personal cost. No extra paycheck is invented.

choices.label: Share the load with colleagues
choices.text: Spend time building a temporary rotation.
choices.feedback: The rotation spreads the pressure. It still asks more of an already stretched team.

title: A temporary reduction in paid hours
prompt: Demand falls. In this scenario your employer reduces paid hours for part of the year. All options involve less income; the choice is how to manage the disruption.
context: This is a fictional workplace event; it is not a forecast about your occupation.

choices.label: Accept the reduced schedule
choices.text: Lose $4,000 gross this year; use the time to search for stable work.
choices.feedback: Your bills continue while pay falls. Time spent searching does not produce a guaranteed job.

choices.label: Pick up temporary shifts elsewhere
choices.text: Lose only $1,800 gross overall, but take on an irregular schedule.
choices.feedback: Extra work replaces part of the missing income and leaves little recovery time.

choices.label: Use the time for a low-cost course
choices.text: Lose $4,000 gross and spend $250 on learning.
choices.feedback: You build skills while the immediate budget becomes harder to balance.

title: A promotion with a price
prompt: A supervisory trial would add $3,500 gross for this year. It also involves conflict resolution and an on-call rotation. You can decline without losing your existing job.
context: The trial raise is limited to this year; continuing management pay is not assumed.

choices.label: Try the supervisory role
choices.text: Take the trial pay and the on-call commitment.
choices.feedback: You practice leadership and earn more, while the schedule reaches into personal time.

choices.label: Ask for a smaller project-lead role
choices.text: Receive $1,200 gross and lead a defined project.
choices.feedback: The smaller trial has a smaller payoff and a more limited responsibility.

choices.label: Stay in your current role
choices.text: Keep the existing workload and pay.
choices.feedback: You protect the kind of work and schedule you prefer. Promotion is not the only useful direction.

title: A required work expense
prompt: Your employer requires updated work equipment. In this story, reimbursement covers only part of the cost. You must arrange an acceptable solution before next month.
context: Specific equipment depends on the occupation; these prices are classroom assumptions.

choices.label: Buy the new equipment
choices.text: Pay the $600 remaining cost after reimbursement.
choices.feedback: The equipment is ready and your cash buffer is smaller.

choices.label: Use an approved refurbished option
choices.text: Pay $300 and accept a shorter expected lifespan.
choices.feedback: You meet the requirement at a lower cost. Replacement may come sooner.

choices.label: Use the employer loan pool
choices.text: Pay $75 in handling costs and coordinate a shared schedule.
choices.feedback: You avoid a large purchase but lose flexibility in when the equipment is available.

title: Boundaries with a demanding client
prompt: Someone expects responses outside your scheduled hours. Your supervisor wants the relationship maintained but has not promised additional pay.
context: There is no extra income for unpaid availability in this scenario.

choices.label: Set a clear response schedule
choices.text: Explain when to expect a reply and provide an escalation route.
choices.feedback: A clear agreement helps protect time. Some difficult conversations remain.

choices.label: Stay available every evening
choices.text: Keep the client satisfied by remaining on call informally.
choices.feedback: The relationship improves for now, but unpaid work takes over personal time.

choices.label: Build a shared coverage plan
choices.text: Coordinate with colleagues and review it with your supervisor.
choices.feedback: Shared coverage reduces individual pressure and still needs everyone’s time.

title: Your skills need an update
prompt: A new process changes how your team works. You can learn during limited work hours, pay for guided help, or continue using the old approach for a while.
context: Change creates both learning opportunities and transition costs.

choices.label: Use the scheduled practice sessions
choices.text: Learn gradually and accept a temporary drop in output.
choices.feedback: You build a foundation while producing less during the transition.

choices.label: Pay for guided practice
choices.text: Spend $450 and practice after work.
choices.feedback: Extra help speeds the transition at a cost in cash and time.

choices.label: Delay learning the new process
choices.text: Keep the familiar routine for now.
choices.feedback: Your short-term routine is easier, but more tasks are moving to the new system.
